prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms enabled frequency measurement at the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock first, and the opening ballots strengthen that view. Four colleagues (Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson and Johansson) independently describe the same chain: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium lattice clock, then Ye's group taking accuracy and stability to the low 1e-18 level. That is a single, well-defined achievement with a clean two-name attribution, which none of the other leading candidates has (B006 forces a choice among four names, B009 among five, B038 leaves out the HgTe theory proposers). It is an instrument-level result, confirmed by many independent laboratories in several atomic species through direct clock-to-clock comparison, which is the strongest form of verification an experiment can have. Its consequences are concrete: the pending redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy, and sensitivity to variations of fundamental constants and dark-sector couplings. As a builder of detectors, I weigh a measurement capability that keeps producing new physics more than a result whose value rests on a model.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap and timing. The 2005 prize (frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, control of single quantum systems, including ion clocks) already honoured adjacent technology, and a reader could see the lattice clock as an incremental step in precision spectroscopy. Other groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Schmidt and the Yb community) made essential contributions that the two-name credit omits, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. There is also a real question of whether the Prize should reward the idea (Katori) more than the record-setting realization (Ye), since Ye's contribution was a long-term accuracy programme more than a separate invention.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as the clearest case where a laser-spectroscopy technique changed what can be measured, argues the two-name configuration is clean and should not be widened, but flags overlap with the comb and ion-clock prizes.
responses.response: I agree with the two-name configuration and with not widening it. I would go further on the overlap worry: the 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured the comb and single-ion control, but neither contains the magic-wavelength idea, which removes the light shift on the clock transition while keeping a large number of atoms. That is what let neutral-atom clocks reach 1e-18 stability in short averaging times, and the ion clocks do not do that. I part company with you on B009. You rank it second, but I think the five-name credit set and the 2001 lineage make it a weaker second choice than B038 or B042, where the allocation is at least tractable.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first on atomic-structure grounds (polarizabilities, blackbody shifts) and asks whether recognition should wait until the second is redefined, and whether Ye's role is a realization rather than a co-invention.
responses.response: I would not wait for the redefinition. The Prize has never required that a technology be adopted as a standard; it requires a discovery or invention of great benefit, and the clock comparisons at the 1e-18 level already show that benefit in measurement. Waiting also adds risk, since the redefinition timetable is set by metrology bodies rather than by physics merit. On Ye, I accept your qualification in part. The citation I propose says 'invention and realization' so that both roles are honoured, with Katori as the originator of the magic-wavelength concept and Ye as the person who made the clocks reach the accuracy and who developed the many-body clock work. I would still keep Ye, because without the accuracy record the idea would remain a proposal.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks time-reversal-invariant topological insulators first, regards the concept as general and overdue, and notes that the 2D and 3D cases involve experimentalists and theorists outside the credited names.
responses.response: I take B038 seriously and keep it as my first alternative, since four members put it in their top three. But your own caveat is exactly why I rank it below the clock. The credited names omit Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang for the HgTe prediction, and the 3D experiments are outside the entry, so the committee would have to decide which of two incomplete stories it is telling. The 2016 prize on topological phases also sits close to it. If the committee finds the clock unconvincing, I would rather give Kane, Mele and Molenkamp a prize than reopen the clock case, but I think the attribution problem is more serious than the opening ballots suggest.

responses.point: Olsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, arguing it has a precise falsifiable origin and large downstream impact, and says the prize should rest on the flat-band prediction and correlated states rather than on the mechanism of superconductivity.
responses.response: I ranked B042 seventh and want to be fair to it. Your point that the prize can rest on the flat-band prediction and the observation of correlated insulators, without taking a position on the pairing mechanism, is a sound way to frame it, and the reproducibility across many groups is real. My reservation is timing and attribution: the experiments are about eight years old, Cao and Fatemi did much of the measurement without being credited, and earlier continuum-model work (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) is part of the history. I regard it as a strong prize for a few years from now rather than the best choice today, and I keep it as my second alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes as leaving enough room for a lattice-clock prize.
Whether Katori and Ye should both be credited as inventors, or the citation should distinguish concept from realization; I am recalling the early strontium history from memory.
Whether other clock groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Yb lattice clocks) are important enough that a two-name prize would be seen as unfair.
Whether a timing argument based on the pending redefinition of the second should delay the award.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the preferred B046 configuration. My documented connections are to PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur, which are astroparticle collaborations; this matters only for B025 (IceCube), which I ranked third in my opening and am not proposing, and I would consider recusal from any decision on that candidate.
